blocks.text: **The write amplification problem:** data gets written to memtable → SSTable → merged again during compaction → maybe again. A byte may be written 10–20 times. This is the fundamental cost of LSM and the reason for leveled vs. size-tiered compaction policies.
**When you must know the LSM:** when you pick a database (RocksDB-backed DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB WiredTiger, etcd, CockroachDB) and when you evaluate write-heavy ingestion workloads.

blocks.text: **HNSW in one paragraph:** build a multi-layer proximity graph. The top layer has few nodes and long edges (for fast long-range jumps); the bottom layer has all nodes and short edges (for precise local search). A query starts at the top layer and greedily moves to the nearest neighbor, descending layer by layer. Search is O(log N)-ish, with a tunable `ef` (recall vs. speed) and `M` (graph degree).

blocks.text: If you issue 100 requests to 10 servers, one of which is slow, the average tells you nothing and the p99 tells you the truth.
**The math:** with `n` servers and one slow server, the probability a request hits the slow one is `1/n`. With 10,000 requests, ~1,000 hit it. The p99 is dominated by the slow server.

items.text: **A slow server** (noisy neighbor, degraded disk, GC pause).
**Queueing** — the request waited in a queue before being served.
**Lock contention** — waiting for a shared resource.
**GC pauses** — the JVM/Go runtime stops the world.
**Network variance** and retransmits.
**Cold caches** — a new instance must warm up.
**Cold storage** — the first read from a spinning disk or a cold S3 object.
**Cross-region variance.**

blocks.text: Because a second independent draw is likely to hit a fast path, the p99 of the *hedged* result approaches the p50 of a single request. Cost: up to 2x load during slow periods — acceptable because slow periods are rare.
**Important caveat:** hedging is only safe for **idempotent** reads. Never hedge a write (unless it's idempotent with a key).
**The biggest performance lever is usually not the algorithm — it's the access pattern.**

sections.title: 10. Time and space complexity cheat sheet for system design

items.text: **Implement a bloom filter.** Build it with 10 bits/element, test 1M inserted elements and 1M non-members, measure the actual false positive rate against the theoretical value. Then implement a counting bloom filter and show deletion working.
**Implement an LSM tree.** A memtable + 2 SSTables, with a compaction that merges them. Compare write and read performance against a B-tree (e.g. SQLite) for an insert-heavy workload.
**Implement consistent hashing vs. modulo hashing.** Ch. 03 exercise 1 — measure how many keys move when the server count changes from 10 to 11.
**Implement HNSW (simplified).** Build a graph, insert vectors, search with `ef` tuning. Compare recall and latency against brute force for 100k vectors. Plot recall vs. `ef`.

**Demonstrate tail latency.** Run a local server, add an artificial slow endpoint (200 ms), and fire 10,000 requests at 10 instances. Show the average vs. p99. Then implement hedged requests and show the p99 improvement and the added load.
**Implement a token bucket in memory** and compare its behavior under bursty vs. smooth traffic against a fixed window.

blocks.text: Good: "For the feed I'd use a sorted set keyed by (user, score) — sorted by score for ranking and by time for the recency window. For 100M users I'd shard by user ID with consistent hashing so a user's feed is co-located. For the hot celebrity case I'd pull their fan-out into a separate sorted set to avoid a write hotspot."

Better: "I'd use an LSM-backed store for the write-heavy ingest path and a B-tree index for the point lookups. For the recommendation lookup I'd use HNSW with int8 quantization to keep the index in memory, and I'd measure recall against brute force to pick `ef`. And I'd add hedged requests on the read path because our p99 is dominated by queueing, not by service time."
Red flags: confusing B-tree with hash; not knowing what a bloom filter is; ignoring tail latency; not being able to explain the write/read trade-off of LSM.

selfCheck.q: **Why do databases use B-trees instead of hash tables for indexes?**
selfCheck.a: Because indexes need **range scans, sorting, and ordered iteration** — a hash table offers none of those. A B-tree also minimizes disk I/O with a high fanout (3–4 levels for billions of rows) and stores keys in sorted order.

selfCheck.q: **What is the LSM tree's write path, and what is its main cost?**
selfCheck.a: Writes go to an in-memory memtable (fast, sequential); when it fills, it's flushed to a sorted immutable run (SSTable) on disk; background compaction merges runs. The main cost is **write amplification** — a byte may be rewritten many times during compaction.

selfCheck.q: **Write amplification in an LSM — what causes it and what's the trade-off?**
selfCheck.a: Overlapping runs must be merged; with size-tiered compaction the merge cost grows quickly, with leveled compaction it's more constant but does more work per merge. The trade-off is **write amplification vs. read amplification** and vs. space usage.

selfCheck.q: **What does a bloom filter guarantee and not guarantee?**
selfCheck.a: It **guarantees no false negatives** (if an element is present, `contains` returns true) and allows **false positives** (says "maybe present" for something that isn't). That's exactly what makes it useful as a pre-filter before an expensive lookup.

selfCheck.q: **Why can't you delete from a standard bloom filter, and what's the fix?**
selfCheck.a: Clearing a bit could remove a bit shared with another element, creating a false negative. Fix: use a **counting bloom filter** (a counter per position instead of a bit) and decrement on delete, or use a **cuckoo filter**.

selfCheck.q: **What is consistent hashing, and what problem does it solve?**
selfCheck.a: It minimizes data movement when the cluster size changes. With `hash(key) % N`, adding a server remaps ~all keys; with consistent hashing, only ~1/N move.

selfCheck.q: **Compare HRW (rendezvous) hashing with a consistent hash ring.**
selfCheck.a: **Ring + virtual nodes:** keys and servers are placed on a ring; keys map clockwise. Requires virtual nodes for even distribution. **HRW:** for each key, compute `hash(key, server)` for every server and pick the max — no ring, no virtual nodes, minimal metadata, excellent distribution, but O(N) computation per lookup. HRW is generally preferred in modern systems.

selfCheck.q: **What is a CRDT, and what three properties must it have?**
selfCheck.a: A data type whose concurrent updates converge to the same value on all replicas without coordination. It must have a **commutative**, **associative**, and **idempotent** merge.

selfCheck.q: **What does HNSW stand for and what is the core idea?**
selfCheck.a: **Hierarchical Navigable Small World.** A multi-layer proximity graph: a sparse top layer for long-range jumps and a dense bottom layer for precise local search. A query greedily moves to the nearest neighbor, descending layer by layer — roughly O(log N).

selfCheck.q: **What are the three axes of the vector-search trade-off?**
selfCheck.a: **Recall, latency, and memory.** Higher recall generally costs latency (bigger `ef`, bigger graph) or memory (more edges, larger quantization). Quantization trades recall for memory.

selfCheck.q: **What is a hedged request and why does it reduce p99?**
selfCheck.a: Because the second draw is independent: if the first request is stuck in a queue or on a slow node, a second request to another node is likely to hit a fast path. The result is that the hedged p99 approaches the unhedged p50 — a large improvement, at the cost of extra load during slow periods.

selfCheck.q: **Why must hedged requests only be used for idempotent operations?**
selfCheck.a: Hedging means the same logical operation may be executed twice concurrently. For a non-idempotent operation (a charge, an increment, a send), that means a duplicate effect. Only hedge reads, or writes protected by an idempotency key.

selfCheck.q: **What is queue-aware (LIFO) load balancing and why does it help?**
selfCheck.a: Least-recently-used routing can send traffic to a busy server, adding queueing delay. LIFO routing prefers the server with the shortest queue (or the one most recently idle), reducing queueing delay and therefore tail latency.

selfCheck.q: **Why is sequential I/O so much faster than random I/O?**
selfCheck.a: Because the read/write head can move sequentially across the medium, avoiding a seek; modern NVMe SSDs get high throughput from parallel channels. Random I/O requires a seek (or a parallel random-access protocol), which is much slower per operation.

selfCheck.q: **What is a count-min sketch good for, and what is its characteristic error?**
selfCheck.a: Finding the **heavy hitters** (most frequent items) in a stream with sublinear space (count-min sketch). Its characteristic error is that it **never overestimates** — it only underestimates (by at most the standard error).

selfCheck.q: **What is HyperLogLog good for?**
selfCheck.a: Estimating the **cardinality** (number of distinct elements) of a stream with ~16 KB and ~0.81% error. Used for unique visitors/users.

selfCheck.q: **What does Redis use a skip list for, and why?**
selfCheck.a: Redis uses skip lists for **sorted sets (ZSETs)** — to order members by score and answer range queries (e.g. "top 10 by score", "members in score range 100–200"). Skip lists give O(log n) with relatively simple, lock-friendly implementation.

selfCheck.q: **Name four sources of tail latency.**
selfCheck.a: A slow server, queueing delay, lock contention, GC pauses, network variance/retransmits, cold caches, cold storage (first read from disk or a cold object), and cross-region variance.

selfCheck.q: **What is MinHash used for?**
selfCheck.a: **Near-duplicate detection** — estimating the Jaccard similarity of sets (e.g. finding near-duplicate web pages or documents) by hashing the sets' elements into a fixed-size signature.

selfCheck.q: **How does a consistent hash ring help during a rebalance?**
selfCheck.a: Because only the keys owned by the departing or joining server need to move; the ring's membership change is localized, so the rebalance touches ~1/N of the data rather than remapping everything.
